simulation_brief.summary: A fictional public-housing authority is preparing elevator repairs that will require temporary relocation for some residents. The initial state includes institutional planning, resident concern, a disability-rights complaint, a mayoral public statement, and rumor-heavy social posting. Key uncertainties center on whether relocation is implemented with sufficient support, delayed by operational or political pressure, escalates into protest, or triggers legal/administrative intervention.

sociology_baseline.description: Residents are more likely to update beliefs from trusted intermediaries like the association or familiar neighbors than from distant official assurances alone.
Many residents remain inactive until visible signs of mistreatment, inaccessible relocation, or peer participation cross a threshold.
Dependency on the housing authority and fear of retaliation or futility suppress some public dissent despite private concern.
Residents sort information through disability status, floor-level experience, and neighbor trust networks, producing uneven interpretations.
Protest or complaint participation becomes more likely if concerns are echoed by the association, advocates, and peers simultaneously.
Resident identity and fairness norms can strengthen solidarity, while outside political framing may create us-versus-them narratives.
Broader city attention is likely to fade quickly unless conflict, visible hardship, or legal escalation produces new hooks.

sociology_prompt_influences.description: Residents rely materially on the authority for continued housing and relocation support, increasing compliance pressure and private caution.
Elevator disruption creates heightened stakes for mobility-impaired residents and makes accommodation adequacy a central legitimacy test.
Unverified social posts can outpace official clarification and inflate perceived worst-case scenarios.
If schedule details and relocation criteria remain unclear, suspicion may rise faster than procedural assurances.
Mayoral statements, association messaging, and advocacy complaints provide competing cues about whether the plan is responsible or dangerous.
